The examples narrow the new task to exactly two possible answer sets, and nothing in them decides between the two. I give one set below at 50% confidence.

**Which bit each Y component picks**
- **Y3 is bit 4.** In X5-Y3-Z1, red appears exactly when bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y1 is bit 3.** In X6-Y1-Z2, yellow appears exactly when bit 3 is 0 in both stimuli. X1-Y1-Z3 fits this too: red appears exactly when the two bit-3 values are the same.
- **Y2 is bit 2.** X4-Y2-Z1 fits this with the same rule as X4-Y3-Z1.

**Possible meanings of X and Z**

Z1 gives green for one result and red for the other. Which way round it goes splits everything into two cases.

| | Case A (Z1: true → green) | Case B (Z1: true → red) |
|---|---|---|
| X5 | not both are 1 | both are 1 |
| X2 | both are 1 | not both are 1 |
| X4 | exactly one is 1 | both are the same |
| X1 | both are the same | exactly one is 1 |

Both cases check out against all six known tasks. In both, X1 and X4 come out different, as they must.

X6 is either "neither is 1" with Z2 giving true → yellow, or "at least one is 1" with Z2 giving true → blue. Both fit, and neither clashes with the rules already used, in either case.

That makes 4 assignments that fit all the examples.

**Effect on the new task X5-Y1-Z2 (looks at bit 3)**
- Case A, X6 = "neither": bit 3 is 1 in both → blue; otherwise yellow.
- Case A, X6 = "at least one": both → yellow; otherwise blue.
- Case B, X6 = "neither": both → yellow; otherwise blue.
- Case B, X6 = "at least one": both → blue; otherwise yellow.

So there are two prediction sets, each backed by two assignments. Only inputs 11 and 16 have bit 3 equal to 1 in both stimuli. I chose "both → blue, otherwise yellow"; the other set swaps every colour.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: yellow, green, red, or blue. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> red` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is red.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
